passage: Santosh's diary, Monday, after school. Hansa Ma'am was standing at the door this morning with her hands on her hips, and I thought, Uh-oh, she's angry that we're late. My stomach dropped and I stopped walking. But then she said, in her usual bright voice, “Good morning, quiz champions! Ready for the quiz?” She was catching her breath after climbing three floors with the papers. I had made up the whole angry thing. I think I'll listen to the words first next time, not only look at her hands. 😅

qa.q: How many floors had Hansa Ma'am climbed with the papers?
qa.a: She had climbed three floors.

qa.q: What did Santosh first think Hansa Ma'am's hands on her hips meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: Santosh first thought it meant she was angry that they were late. It turned out she was catching her breath after the stairs, and her bright words showed she was not angry.

qa.q: What can Santosh do next time?
qa.a: Listen to the words and tone as well as looking at her hands, as planned, and wait a moment before deciding she is upset.

qa.q: How might Hansa Ma'am feel if she knew the class had feared she was angry?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised and a little amused, since she was only resting after the climb. She might be glad to reassure them with her cheerful voice.

grounding: A teacher's hands on hips can look like authority or impatience but may be resting; tone and words add meaning.

passage: In the schoolyard of the village school, Saurabh Sir stood with his hands on his hips while the children ran back in from the well. Sonali slowed down. Sir is going to shout, she thought. Some children kept running. But Sir looked at the sky and said in a calm voice, “Clouds are coming. Line up, everyone, quickly, and we'll finish the lesson under the banyan.” His hands dropped as he waved them toward the tree. Sonali let out a breath. He had only been watching the sky.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh Sir tell the children to finish the lesson?
qa.a: He told them to finish the lesson under the banyan.

qa.q: What did Sonali first think Saurabh Sir's hands on his hips meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: She thought he was about to shout, and she slowed down. It turned out he was watching the sky and thinking about the weather.

qa.q: What could Sonali do next time she is unsure about a stance like that?
qa.a: Wait for his words and tone before deciding, and if she is unsure, ask calmly.

qa.q: How might Saurabh Sir see his own stance?
qa.a: As just standing and watching the sky, without realising it looked stern to some children.

grounding: A teacher's hands on hips can read as impatience but may mean nothing; tone and words give the meaning.

passage: On the playground in Edinburgh, Soo-ah was the last to come in from lunch. Ms Freya Campbell stood at the door with both hands on her hips. Soo-ah froze. At her old school, that pose meant trouble. She walked slowly, head down, ready for a scolding. Then Ms Campbell spoke, breathing hard. “Phew! I just ran the three-legged race with Year 4. I'm puffed out.” She was grinning, cheeks pink, and her hands stayed on her hips while she caught her breath. “Come in, Soo-ah. Did you see us fall over?” Soo-ah's shoulders came down, and she laughed.

qa.q: What race had Ms Campbell just run?
qa.a: She had just run the three-legged race with Year 4.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling when she saw the hands on hips?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt scared and ready for a scolding, because at her old school that pose meant trouble.

qa.q: Which cues showed Soo-ah the pose meant resting?
qa.a: Ms Campbell's heavy breathing, grin, pink cheeks and friendly words showed she was catching her breath, not angry.

qa.q: What would change if Ms Campbell had not spoken?
qa.a: Soo-ah might have gone in believing she was in trouble and felt anxious all afternoon.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's hands on hips as impatience when tone and words show she was resting.

passage: At lights-out in the school hostel, Vikas Sir stood at the end of the corridor with his hands on his hips. Simran, still whispering to her bunkmate through the open door, stopped mid-sentence. Hands on hips means he's fed up. Then he spoke, quiet and even: “Ten o'clock. Lights off in two minutes, please.” Not shouting. Not smiling either. Simran studied him: feet planted, voice calm, eyes moving from door to door, counting. It was his in-charge pose, she decided. Not angry, just firm. She switched off her lamp. “Good night, Sir.” “Good night, Simran.”

qa.q: How long did Vikas Sir give before lights off?
qa.a: He gave two minutes before lights off.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she first saw the hands on hips?
qa.a: She felt nervous, thinking he was fed up with the whispering.

qa.q: How did Simran work out what the pose meant?
qa.a: She added his calm, even voice, planted feet and counting eyes to the pose, and read it as firm authority, not anger.

qa.q: How might Vikas Sir see his own stance?
qa.a: He probably sees it as a normal way to stand while checking rooms, not as a sign of anger.

grounding: Shows a child reading an adult's hands on hips as impatience, then using tone and words to read it as authority.

passage: I'm Gargi. At kabaddi practice on Tuesday, Coach stood at the edge of the mat with both hands on her hips while Hansa did her raid. Hansa got tagged out, looked over, and her face fell. She walked back slowly, muttering, “She's annoyed with me.” I wasn't sure. Coach's voice, when it came, was cheerful: “Nice footwork, Hansa! Again!” Then Coach pressed her hands into her lower back and stretched, wincing a little. “Old back,” she said. Hansa looked at me. I shrugged. Maybe the hands had just been holding up her back all along.

qa.q: What did Coach say after Hansa's raid?
qa.a: Coach said, “Nice footwork, Hansa! Again!”

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she walked back muttering?
qa.a: Hansa felt discouraged and worried that Coach was annoyed with her.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time she sees that pose?
qa.a: She could wait for Coach's words and tone, or ask, before deciding the hands on hips mean impatience.

qa.q: How did Gargi read Coach's pose?
qa.a: Gargi wasn't sure, and later thought the hands might just have been supporting Coach's sore back.

grounding: Shows a child reading a coach's hands on hips as impatience, when words and tone suggest resting a sore back.

passage:
Tuesday: Nandini Ma'am stood at the classroom door, hands on hips, as Deepika's group raced in after the bell. "Four minutes late," she said, sharp and flat. Deepika slid into her seat. So hands on hips means trouble.

Friday: On sports day, Nandini Ma'am stood by the finish line, hands on hips again, but she was laughing and cheering, "Go, go, go!" Deepika frowned. Trouble didn't cheer.

The next Monday, during the maths test, Nandini Ma'am walked the rows and stopped beside Deepika's desk, hands on hips. Deepika's pencil froze. Then Ma'am stretched backwards with a small groan. "Too much bending over copies," she murmured to nobody. Deepika almost laughed and went back to her sums.

qa.q: How late were Deepika's group on Tuesday?
qa.a: Four minutes late.

qa.q: Why did Deepika's pencil freeze during the maths test?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of worry, reading Ma'am's hands on hips as annoyance, as it had been on Tuesday.

qa.q: What helped Deepika read the gesture more accurately over time?
qa.a: Noticing the tone and words that came with it: sharp words meant impatience, cheering meant excitement, and a groan and stretch meant a sore back.

qa.q: What was Nandini Ma'am actually going through during the test?
qa.a: Her back ached from bending over copies, so she was stretching and resting, not annoyed with Deepika.

grounding: It shows a child reading a teacher's hands on hips as impatience, then learning from tone and words that it can mean cheering or simply resting.
